title: Cell-autonomous inflammation in VEXAS is mediated by ERAD failure and cGAS–STING - Nature Cell Biology
byline: Magaziner; Samuel J; Collins; Jason C; Zheng; Patrick; Bertulfo; Kalay; Miller; Brecca; Wang; Amy K; Hadjadj; Jerome; Balandrán; Juan Carlos; Sirenko; Maria; En
html:
Abstract

VEXAS (vacuoles, E1 enzyme, X-linked, autoinflammatory and somatic) is a severe adult-onset inflammatory disease caused by somatic mutations that reduce cytoplasmic activity of UBA1, the primary initiating enzyme for ubiquitylation. How this hypomorphic state drives cell-intrinsic immune activation in mature myeloid cells is unknown. Using unbiased multi-omic, biochemical and cell biological analyses of model systems and patient-derived cells, we show that loss of cytoplasmic UBA1 activity convergently disrupts endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation (ERAD) and mitochondrial homeostasis. ERAD failure arises from preferential undercharging of ERAD E2 enzymes, explaining hallmark VEXAS features, including endoplasmic reticulum-derived vacuoles and unfolded protein response activation, and promotes accumulation of the ERAD substrate STING. Simultaneously, mitochondrial dysfunction is associated with cytosolic leakage of mitochondrial DNA, cGAS-dependent STING signalling and inflammatory cytokine production. STING inhibition or reversal of mitochondrial DNA leakage resolves multi-cytokine inflammation in VEXAS models and patient myeloid cells, establishing the cGAS–STING pathway as a therapeutically actionable vulnerability.

Main

Systemic autoinflammatory diseases are monogenic disorders that cause constitutive activation of the innate immune system1. VEXAS (vacuoles, E1 enzyme, X-linked, autoinflammatory and somatic) is a severe, late-onset autoinflammatory condition that affects 1 in 4,000 males over 50 years of age2,3. VEXAS is caused by somatic, hypomorphic mutations in haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) in the UBA1 gene, which encodes the E1 enzyme responsible for initiating the majority of ubiquitylation4. The disease-causing mutations in VEXAS are restricted to the haematopoietic system, most prominently in the myeloid lineage. Patients with VEXAS have severe inflammation, which can affect various organs, including the skin, lungs and joints, along with haematological conditions such as pancytopenia and myelodysplastic syndrome5,6. VEXAS is associated with substantially increased mortality and highly effective treatments are currently lacking7.

UBA1 is ubiquitously expressed and functions as the initial enzyme in the ubiquitin-proteasome system, charging most ubiquitin-conjugating (E2) enzymes in the cell8. As a result, UBA1 is pivotal for processes such as the cell cycle, proliferation, growth and dynamic responses to stimuli. Ubiquitylation is also essential for maintaining a balanced proteome by facilitating the degradation of unnecessary or misfolded proteins through mechanisms such as autophagy-mediated degradation, the endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation (ERAD) pathway and the unfolded protein response (UPR)9,10,11.

Most VEXAS-causing mutations occur at p.Met41 and result in the loss of cytoplasmic UBA1 activity through decreased translation of the cytoplasmic isoform or are characterized by impaired E2 enzyme charging12,13. Bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) from cells of patients with VEXAS have revealed pronounced inflammation, particularly within the myeloid lineage14,15,16. This inflammation is characterized by the activation of the type I interferon pathway and other pro-inflammatory cytokines (for example, interleukin (IL)-6 and tumour necrosis factor (TNF)). Furthermore, these studies have identified concomitant activation of the UPR, which has been implicated as a downstream mechanism of inflammation in disorders related to ubiquitylation, including proteasomopathies14,17,18,19. Recent work has also elucidated the role of aberrant TNF-dependent cell death in non-cell-autonomous inflammation and propagating systemic disease pathologies20,21. However, because TNF blockade is not effective in treating patients with VEXAS7 and existing mutant models do not show spontaneous cell death15,22,23 additional cell-intrinsic upstream mechanisms must initiate and maintain inflammation. In this study, we utilized multiple complementary cellular models and patient-derived samples to define how loss of cytoplasmic UBA1 activity drives cell-autonomous inflammation in mutant myeloid lineages. Our data identify the central role of ERAD failure and mitochondrial dysfunction as key upstream events that converge on cGAS–STING activation, thereby initiating and sustaining VEXAS-associated inflammation.

Results

UBA1 pathogenic variants lead to inflammation, ERAD dysregulation, UPR activation and vesicle disruption

To dissect the molecular events driving inflammation in VEXAS myeloid cells, before the pleiotropic effects and adaptation after loss of ubiquitylation and without the complexities of patient-derived tissues, we developed an inducible in vitro model (Extended Data Fig. 1a). This system uses human THP1 monocytes/macrophages engineered to undergo CRISPR–Cas9-mediated deletion of endogenous UBA1 upon induction with doxycycline (dox), complemented with either UBA1WT or UBA1M41V (Fig. 1a). Our VEXAS model, THP1 UBA1M41V, successfully recapitulated key disease features, including the cytoplasmic isoform switch from active UBA1b to catalytically impaired UBA1c (Fig. 1b and Extended Data Fig. 1b), reduced global ubiquitylation (Fig. 1b and Extended Data Fig. 1b), UPR activation (Fig. 1b and Extended Data Fig. 1c), vacuole formation (Extended Data Fig. 1d, e) and inflammation corresponding with VEXAS hallmark pathways (for example, type I interferon, IL-6 and TNF) that was present in the monocyte and more pronounced in the macrophage state (Fig. 1b–d and Extended Data Fig. 1c) at day 9 post-induction with doxycycline. Notably, no spontaneous apoptosis, pyroptosis or necroptosis was observed in THP1 UBA1M41V monocytes or macrophages despite robust inflammation (Fig. 1b), suggesting that cell-intrinsic pathways are required to initiate inflammation in VEXAS myeloid cells.

To identify such pathways in an unbiased manner, we conducted transcriptomic, proteomic and ubiquitylated protein enrichment analyses in both THP1 UBA1M41V and monocytes derived from patients with VEXAS (Supplementary Fig. 1, Extended Data Fig. 2 and Supplementary Tables 1–5). Compared with their control counterparts, both patient-derived and model cells exhibited highly correlated dysregulated pathways, further confirming that THP1 UBA1M41V cells faithfully replicate key features of VEXAS (Extended Data Fig. 2a). Focusing on pathways enriched in VEXAS CD14+ monocytes, we identified shared activation of inflammatory signalling and the UPR in both the THP1 model and patient cells (Fig. 1e, Extended Data Fig. 2b and Supplementary Table 1). These findings are consistent with previous studies using patient samples14,18.

Given the role of UBA1 in post-translational regulation and the stronger correlation between model and patient datasets at the proteomic level (Extended Data Fig. 2a), we next focused on proteomic pathways enriched in both patient and THP1 UBA1M41V monocytes (Fig. 1e–g and Supplementary Tables 2 and 3). While inflammatory and UPR pathways were identified as expected in transcriptomic analyses, ERAD, Golgi transport and mitochondrial regulation emerged among the most enriched pathways, with many critical proteins showing significant enrichment compared with controls (Fig. 1f, g). Immunoblotting and immunofluorescence of the THP1 UBA1M41V model validated these findings, confirming endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and dysregulated ERAD and Golgi vesicle transport (Fig. 1h and Extended Data Fig. 1g). Additionally, bulk and scRNA-seq data from patient monocytes corroborated deregulation of ERAD pathways in VEXAS (Extended Data Fig. 3a, b and Supplementary Tables 4 and 5). We made similar observations in scRNA-seq datasets from patients’ HSPCs (Extended Data Fig. 3b). Using a base editor approach, we constructed an HSPC model of VEXAS, in which the UBA1M41T mutation is introduced into CD34+ donor HSPCs15,18,24 and also found that ERAD was the top dysregulated Gene Ontology biological processes (GOBP) pathway in proteomic analyses along with dysregulated pathways, suggesting possible mitochondrial dysfunction, such as reactive oxygen species metabolism and the electron transport chain (Extended Data Fig. 3c–e).

Taken together, through unbiased approaches, our inducible model of VEXAS successfully reproduces dysregulated pathways observed in patient cells and identifies ERAD dysfunction and mitochondrial dysregulation as early disease signals in VEXAS pathogenesis.

ERAD failure precedes inflammation and results from a preferential loss of ubiquitin charging to ER-tethered E2s

To further delineate the stepwise pathways causing inflammation in VEXAS, we monitored the proteomes of our THP1 model at different time periods after replacement of endogenous UBA1 with either UBA1WT or UBA1M41V (Supplementary Fig. 1a,b). Notably, ERAD- and UPR-related pathways and proteins were significantly enriched in VEXAS model cells before the onset of inflammation (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Table 6), suggesting that loss of ERAD function with subsequent activation of the UPR precedes VEXAS inflammation. To test whether ERAD was indeed impaired in VEXAS cells, we utilized a fluorescent (green fluorescent protein; GFP) reporter (CD3δ–GFP), which is degraded through the ERAD pathway (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). In VEXAS THP1 cells, reporter levels were elevated under basal conditions and were not as efficiently degraded upon inhibition of protein translation using cycloheximide (CHX), demonstrating impaired ERAD function (Fig. 2b). We made similar observations for UBA1M41L 32D cells, a recently described constitutive murine cell model of VEXAS (Extended Data Fig. 4c)23. We also observed basal dysregulation of components of the SEL1L–HRD1 complex, the best-characterized mammalian ERAD E3 ligase complex25,26 in VEXAS THP1 cells, as well as stabilization of its endogenous substrates CD147 and OS9 in cycloheximide chase assays (Extended Data Fig. 4d–g). ERAD inhibition using EerI caused selective lethality in VEXAS cell lines, similar to treatment with the UBA1 inhibitor TAK-243, further indicating impairment of the pathway in VEXAS (Supplementary Fig. 2a,b).
